body_markdown:
We live in a very different world today. Customers are already starting to[talk to their banking apps](https://www.starlingbank.com/news/-talk-to-transact-starling-customers-can-use-their-voice-to-send-money/) , and AI agents are starting to[pay on customers’ behalf](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/openai-chatgpt-wallet-dot-purchases.html) . Banks now have to design not only for customers tapping through an app but also for their in-app AI assistants and potentially third-party agents that help those customers decide and act. Our latest review of 22 retail banks’ mobile apps across Australia, Europe, India, and North America found that leaders stand out by helping customers understand what’s happening with their money and act on it.


## Leaders Connect Insight With Action


The leading banks in this year’s review — Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CommBank), Intesa Sanpaolo, IDFC FIRST Bank, and U.S. Bank — let customers complete tasks in the app without redirecting them to another channel or leaving the next step unclear. Our review found three shifts in how banking apps serve customers:


- **Financial insights are becoming more actionable.** Most banking apps can categorize transactions or show customers where their money went. Leaders go further by helping customers decide what to do next. CommBank uses customers’ average spending to create starter budgets and predicts upcoming bills to help them plan. U.S. Bank’s Money Tracker and Balance Forecast show customers not only where their money went but where their balance may be heading — and its automated savings options give them ways to act on those insights.
- **Safeguards are becoming part of the experience.** Leading banks don’t treat security solely as a control that runs in the background. They bring safeguards into the customer journey at the moment a mistake or suspicious action may occur. Intesa Sanpaolo warns customers about apparent duplicate transfers and address errors, as well as asking them to verify potentially costly currency changes. U.S. Bank shows customers a security rating, while IDFC FIRST Bank brings fraud reporting and dispute management into digital servicing.
- **Conversational banking is modestly changing engagement.** Conversational assistants promise a more intuitive way to bank, and current implementations are moving from answering questions to completing tasks. IDFC FIRST Bank’s[FIRST.AI](https://www.spjimr.org/newsroom/event/idfc-first-bank-leadership-talk-ai-in-banking-beyond-the-buzzwords/) lets customers review spending, manage cards, open fixed deposits, and make payments by voice or text. Most conversational assistants, however, still handle narrow use cases. As AI models take on longer, multistep goals, banks must decide whether to give third-party agents controlled access, restrict them, or offer their own alternatives.


## **Decide Where To Invest**


We recommend four investment postures, based on each feature’s customer and business value and how broadly competitors have deployed it:


- **Make table stakes excellent.** Digital self-service, personalized rewards, and payment requests are valuable and widespread enough that poor execution puts a bank at a disadvantage. Banks should remove friction, increase completion rates, and deliver these capabilities consistently.
- **Differentiate where competitors have yet to follow.** Instant virtual cards, contextual suspicious-activity reporting, and personalized investment insights deliver strong value — but only a handful of banks offer them. They give a bank room to stand out, provided it understands the costs, execution risks, and demand in its target segments.
- **Monitor widely offered features that deliver limited value today.** Several banks offer international currency tools and clearer cross-border transfer costs, but these will only drive value if banks’ offerings are as compelling as — if not more compelling than — its competitors. Limit investment unless a feature supports a distinctive proposition that will become market-leading.
- **Test unproven features before you scale them.** Few banks offer subscription management, debt management, and spending views over time — and currently, these features create limited value on their own. Their potential increases when they lead to a useful action, such as canceling a subscription, changing a repayment plan, or preventing a cash-flow shortfall. Banks should run targeted experiments and scale only when the evidence demonstrates customer and business value.
